newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Labour, NZ First to meet, no draft deal yet.
newsitem.headline: Labour, NZ First to meet, no draft deal yet.

text.p: A spokesman for New Zealand Labour Party leader Helen Clark said on Monday there was little likelihood an agreed position or executive summary of a coalition deal with nationalist New Zealand First could be ready in time for Tuesday's scheduled Labour caucus meeting.
Political sources told Reuters that NZ First and the caretaker National Party government appeared to have exhausted their parallel talks for now, and no face to face meetings were planned on Monday.

Senior sources in NZ First said an announcement on a new government was unlikely before Friday. The party has been negotiating to form a government with either National or Labour after inconclusive elections on October 12.
Centre-left Labour and nationalist NZ First negotiators were due to meet at 3 p.m. (0200 GMT), spokesmen for the two parties said.
The two teams of negotiators were to meet face to face last Friday to hammer out the details of an executive summary, but the planned meeting was cancelled by NZ First at the last minute.
"There is no indication it (an executive summary) will be ready by tomorrow," the spokesman for Clark said.
"Labour will not have finalised its discussions (with NZ First) by Tuesday's caucus, so it is premature to talk of summaries being put before the meeting," he said.

Paper work has continued to be exchanged, and NZ First policy coordinator MP Peter McCardle stayed in Wellington at the weekend to continue policy work while NZ First leader Winston Peters hosted a rally in his seat of Tauranga.

NZ First holds the balance of power after the October election. This is the seventh week of talks between NZ First and Labour and the incumbent conservative National government over the shape of the next government.

When it was released, the coalition deal would contain detailed policy agreements and in some cases draft legislation, one source said, adding this would not include the Employment Contracts Act industrial relations law.
He said "reconciliation documents" were being prepared, marrying where possible the different policies of the parties.
